_readme: Golden test set for the evaluation engine (master plan 15.1). Each case asserts a score BAND, not an exact number, so prompt tweaks don't break the suite. expectBand = target with the LLM path live. expectBandDeterministic = what the offline fallback achieves, where it is honestly blunter; the suite asserts whichever mode it ran in. requiresLlm marks a case the deterministic path CANNOT detect -- that is a stated limitation, not a bug to hide. Run tools/calibrate.py to print this as a table for the Q&A slide.

cases.label: Strong answer: correct, complete, concise
cases.questionText: How would you design a secure token-based authentication system using JWTs, and how do you handle token revocation when a user logs out?
cases.answerText: A JWT has a header, payload and signature, and I would keep the access token short-lived at about 15 minutes so a leaked token expires quickly. Alongside it I issue a longer-lived refresh token stored in an httpOnly, secure, sameSite cookie so JavaScript cannot read it. On refresh I use refresh token rotation: each use issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, and if an old one is reused I treat that as theft and revoke the whole family. Because JWTs are stateless I cannot revoke an access token directly, so for logout I keep a denylist of token IDs in Redis with a TTL equal to the remaining token lifetime, and the API checks it on each request.
cases.why: Hits every expected concept with specifics. If this does not land in the top band, the scorer is too harsh and every real answer will look bad.
cases.deterministicNote: Lexical fallback matches 3/5 concepts where embeddings match 5/5, so the offline score sits ~5 points lower. Install sentence-transformers for the real number.

cases.label: Partial: correct but misses an important concept
cases.questionText: How would you design a secure token-based authentication system using JWTs, and how do you handle token revocation when a user logs out?
cases.answerText: I would use a JWT with a header, payload and signature, signed on the server. The access token should be short-lived, maybe 15 minutes, and I would store it in an httpOnly cookie rather than localStorage so it is not exposed to scripts. When it expires the client requests a new one.
cases.why: Correct as far as it goes but never addresses revocation, which is half the question. Must land clearly between the strong and the weak case.

cases.label: CONFIDENT BUT WRONG -- the case that matters most
cases.questionText: What is the difference between a SQL index and a table scan, and when would an index hurt performance?
cases.answerText: An index is a cached copy of the table stored in RAM, so queries read from memory instead of disk, which is why indexes always make a database faster. A table scan means the database has run out of memory and has to go to disk. Adding more indexes therefore always improves performance, and there is no real downside to indexing every column, since writes go to the index first and are flushed later.
cases.why: Uses the right vocabulary and sounds authoritative while being wrong on every claim. This is the documented failure mode of LLM graders -- they score fluency. If our engine puts this above 45 we must say so openly rather than hide it.
cases.deterministicNote: KNOWN LIMITATION, state it openly: the deterministic path verifies that expected concepts are PRESENT, not that claims are TRUE. This answer name-drops the right vocabulary while being wrong on every claim, so it scores ~54 offline. Only the LLM path sets factuallyIncorrect=true, which triggers the 0.55 penalty and drops it below 45. This is the single most likely thing a judge will probe -- lead with it rather than being caught by it.

cases.label: Vague: little evidence
cases.questionText: What is the difference between a SQL index and a table scan, and when would an index hurt performance?
cases.answerText: Indexes are used for performance optimisation in databases. A table scan is slower. It depends on the use case and the requirements of the system.
cases.why: On-topic but substantiates nothing. Must sit below the partial answer.

cases.label: Verbose: relevant but padded and poorly structured
cases.questionText: What is the difference between a SQL index and a table scan, and when would an index hurt performance?
cases.answerText: So basically when we talk about databases there are many things to consider and indexing is one of the most important ones that people talk about a lot in interviews and in real projects also. An index is like the index at the back of a book, you look up the term and it tells you the page, so an index lookup means the database can jump straight to the rows instead of doing a full table scan where it reads every single row one by one which obviously takes longer when the table is big. But there is a cost also because every time you insert or update a row the index has to be updated too, that is write overhead, the B-tree has to be rebalanced and maintained. And if a column has low cardinality, like a status column with only two values, then the index is not very selective so it may not help much at all.
cases.why: Technically strong, badly organised. Should score well on coverage and lose only the clarity component -- padding must not be mistaken for depth, and rambling must not be mistaken for wrongness.
